prompt: What is the main point of the text?
passage:
Anyone who has tried to hold a conversation beside a busy road knows the instinctive remedy: you raise your voice, and perhaps its pitch, until you are heard. Birds, it turns out, do something similar. In many cities, songbirds of several species sing at a higher pitch than their relatives in the quieter countryside, apparently lifting their songs clear of the low rumble of traffic. Some sing more loudly; some start earlier, before the morning rush begins; a few have taken to singing at night, when the streets are quieter.

It is tempting to read such findings as evolution caught in the act, and headlines have rarely resisted the temptation. Cities are young, the argument runs, so any trait that sets urban populations apart must have arisen at remarkable speed. The story appeals because it turns the city, usually cast as nature's enemy, into a laboratory in which natural selection can be watched at work.

The trouble is that a difference between two populations says nothing, on its own, about how the difference came about. A bird that sings higher in a city may carry genes that its rural cousins lack, but it may equally be an ordinary bird doing what birds of its kind have always been able to do: adjusting its song to its surroundings, much as we adjust our voices in a crowded restaurant. Individual birds of some species have been observed raising and lowering their pitch as the noise around them rises and falls, which is hard to square with the idea of a fixed, inherited trait. Telling the two explanations apart requires patient work—raising birds from different populations under identical conditions, for instance—and such studies are slow, expensive and, by the standards of a news cycle, unexciting.

None of this makes urban song less interesting. If anything, the case for flexibility raises a sharper question. Many species have never settled in cities at all, while others have moved in with apparent ease. Perhaps what distinguishes the successful newcomers is not a change acquired after arrival but a capacity they brought with them: a readiness to vary their behaviour when circumstances change. On this view, the city does not so much create new kinds of birds as sort existing ones, admitting those that were adaptable to begin with and quietly turning the rest away.

That is a less dramatic story than evolution at high speed, but it may prove the more useful one. If flexibility is the price of admission, then the species we should worry about as cities spread are not those that already share our streets, but those whose habits are too fixed to follow.
options: Traffic noise has forced urban songbirds to evolve higher-pitched songs in a remarkably short time.
Only slow and patient research can show whether city birds really sing differently from rural ones.
The way city birds sing may say more about adaptability than about rapid genetic change.
City birds may have evolved their flexible way of singing as a response to urban noise.
explain: The author grants that urban birds sing differently but argues that the difference 'says nothing, on its own' about its cause, that it may equally reflect birds adjusting their song, and that such adaptability may also explain which species manage to settle in cities at all, so the songs may say more about adaptability than about rapid genetic change. The idea that traffic noise has forced rapid evolution is the headline reading the author questions. The suggestion that birds evolved their flexibility in response to city noise contradicts the text, which presents flexibility as 'a capacity they brought with them', not 'a change acquired after arrival'. Patient research is said to be needed to tell the two explanations apart, not to establish whether city birds sing differently, which the text treats as an observed fact.

prompt: Why, according to the author, can closer inspection not solve the main problem?
passage:
Every organisation that tries to manage by numbers sooner or later runs into the same awkward fact. A figure that once told you something useful about how well people were working starts, the moment you reward or punish them according to it, to tell you mainly how good they have become at producing that figure. Economists call this Goodhart's law, after the British economist who described it, but few of us need the name. We have all heard of call centres that time their calls and end up with staff who cut difficult customers off, or of schools judged on exam results that quietly stop entering pupils who might fail.

The usual response is outrage, followed by tighter rules. On this account the trouble is cheating: a few unscrupulous individuals game the system, and the cure is closer inspection. Cheating certainly happens, but it is not the heart of the problem. Far more common, and far harder to detect, is the conscientious employee who simply does what she has been asked. Told that her performance will be judged on a single number, she devotes her limited time and attention to that number, and the parts of her job that nobody counts—the patient explanation, the colleague helped out of a tight spot—shrink without anyone ever deciding that they should. No rule has been broken. That is precisely why inspection cannot fix it.

It does not follow that we should throw our measurements away. Organisations that abandon numbers altogether tend to fall back on impressions, and impressions are hardly free of bias; they favour the confident, the visible and the familiar. A hospital that stops recording waiting times does not thereby become kinder to its patients. The question is not whether to measure but what to do with the measurements once we have them.

Here a distinction that is often blurred in practice becomes useful. A number can serve as the start of a conversation or as a verdict. In the first case, a sudden drop in a team's figures prompts someone to go and find out what is happening, and the answer may well be that the team is doing something valuable that the number cannot see. In the second, the same drop sets off an automatic penalty, and the team learns to protect the number rather than explain it. The figures are identical in both cases; what differs is whether anyone is still expected to exercise judgement.

Such judgement does not come cheap. It requires managers who understand the work well enough to see what the numbers leave out, and it cannot be scaled up as easily as a spreadsheet. But the alternative is not objectivity. It is an organisation that knows more and more about less and less.
options: Because conscientious employees hide from inspectors the parts of the job they neglect
Because the problem lies in what people are asked to do, not in people breaking rules
Because inspectors tend to favour the confident, the visible and the familiar
Because cheating has become far too widespread to be investigated properly
explain: The author argues that the main problem is not cheating but the conscientious employee who 'simply does what she has been asked', concentrating on the number she is judged by while the uncounted parts of the job shrink; no rule is broken, which is 'precisely why inspection cannot fix it'. This behaviour is 'far harder to detect' because nothing is being broken, not because employees hide what they neglect; the text says the shrinking happens 'without anyone ever deciding that they should'. The bias towards the confident, the visible and the familiar is attributed to impressions, not to inspectors. And the claim that cheating is too widespread contradicts the statement that cheating 'is not the heart of the problem'.

prompt: What is the main point of the text?
passage: In a famous passage of his Confessions, Augustine describes watching Ambrose, the bishop of Milan, at his reading: his eyes ran over the page and his heart searched out the meaning, but his voice and tongue were still. For generations the scene was cited as proof that silent reading was a rarity in the ancient world—an oddity worth writing down. The inference is weaker than it looks. Ambrose was not alone in a study when Augustine saw him; he read in this way while visitors sat waiting to speak with him. And Augustine's own guesses at the reason—that the bishop wished to avoid being asked to explain difficult passages to his listeners, or to spare a voice that tired easily—concern why a man would read silently in company, not whether such reading was possible. A single surprised witness, in any case, tells us first of all about the witness's own expectations. Whether those expectations were shared by everyone who could read is another question.
options: Silent reading may well have been rarer in antiquity than modern scholars tend to assume.
Augustine misunderstood the reasons why Ambrose chose to read in silence.
Silent reading was in fact widespread in the ancient world, as Augustine's account shows.
Augustine's account says less about ancient reading habits than is often assumed.
explain: The author's central claim is that 'the inference is weaker than it looks': the scene has long been cited as proof that silent reading was rare, but the circumstances and Augustine's own guesses suggest that it shows something narrower. The suggestion that silent reading may have been rarer than modern scholars assume runs against this argument, which weakens the evidence for rarity rather than strengthening it. Nor does the text claim that Augustine misunderstood Ambrose's reasons; his guesses are used as evidence of what puzzled him. Finally, the author does not argue that silent reading was widespread, since whether Augustine's expectations were shared by other readers is left as 'another question'.

prompt: According to the text, why may a document saved thirty years ago be impossible to read today?
passage: A letter left in a drawer for three hundred years can usually still be read by anyone who knows the language. A document saved on a computer thirty years ago may be beyond rescue even if the disk that holds it is in perfect condition. The bits survive; what disappears is everything needed to make sense of them—the program that created the file, the operating system that ran the program, the machine that ran the operating system. Each layer was built on the unspoken assumption that the one beneath it would always be there. Seen this way, preserving digital material has less in common with storing objects than with keeping a language in use. Putting files somewhere safe is only the beginning; someone must go on carrying them over into forms that the tools of the day can open, again and again, for as long as anyone wants them read. A digital archive, in other words, is less a place than an activity.
options: The data on the disk fades gradually, even when the disk itself is well kept.
Modern computers are designed to refuse files made on much older systems.
The programs and machines needed to open it may no longer exist.
No one may still remember what the document was originally for.
explain: The text says that 'the bits survive' and that what disappears is everything needed to make sense of them: 'the program that created the file, the operating system that ran the program, the machine that ran the operating system'. The idea that the data fades contradicts this, as well as the statement that the disk may be in perfect condition. Nothing is said about modern computers being designed to refuse old files; the problem is that the layers needed to read them have disappeared. And 'make sense of them' refers to these technical layers, not to people forgetting what a document was for.

passage: Restaurants that refuse to take bookings like to present the policy as a kind of democracy: no favours for those with connections, first come, first served. prompt: Which of the following would be the most suitable title for the text?
